question.text: Scenario: Pooja Malhotra, a technical analyst at Capital First Securities, is analyzing the Nifty 50 index chart. She observes: (1) Nifty has been in a primary uptrend for the past 18 months, moving from 18,000 to 25,500. (2) Currently, Nifty is forming a Head and Shoulders pattern with Left Shoulder at 25,000, Head at 25,500, and Right Shoulder forming near 25,100. The neckline is at 24,200. (3) The 50-day EMA is at 24,800 and the 200-day EMA is at 23,500. Both are still rising. (4) RSI is at 65, down from 78 two weeks ago. (5) MACD fast line has crossed below the slow line. (6) Volume has been declining on recent up-moves and increasing on down-moves. (7) Sensex is also showing a similar pattern, confirming Dow Theory index confirmation principle. Question 5 of 5: If the neckline at 24,200 breaks with heavy volume, the measured target for the H&S pattern would be approximately:

answer.text: 22,900 — calculated as neckline (24,200) minus the distance from head (25,500) to neckline (1,300)

explanation.text: The Logic: The conventional measured-move target for a confirmed Head and Shoulders top is calculated by taking the vertical distance from the head to the neckline and projecting that same distance downward from the neckline break. Here: head = 25,500, neckline = 24,200, so pattern height = 25,500 - 24,200 = 1,300. Projected downside target = neckline - pattern height = 24,200 - 1,300 = 22,900. This is treated as a minimum objective, not a guaranteed final low. The Trap: 25,500 is the head itself — that is the level being broken away from, not a downside target. 18,000 is the prior cycle low and unrelated to the H&S measured projection. 24,000 is just slightly under the neckline and ignores the pattern-height calculation. Note: The H&S measured-target formula used above is not stated on the cited NISM Series XV Research Analyst pages checked (around pp.295-325, including p.313, which references head-and-shoulders only as a chart pattern for support/resistance identification). The arithmetic is internally correct, and the rule reflects general industry technical-analysis usage rather than the cited workbook chapter.
